items.title: Why a token in localStorage is an XSS risk
items.body:
**Key: any XSS can read the token from browser storage.**

App.tsx saves the whole token response in localStorage under the key netslack.auth when the user signs in. Any JavaScript running on the page can read localStorage. If an attacker manages to inject script into the page (cross-site scripting, XSS), that script can read the token and send it anywhere, then act as the user. The side-effects table records exactly this: browser-side persistence, XSS risk.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Shared with the SignalR server process**: localStorage lives only in the browser; servers never see it unless the page sends it.
- **Sent on every cross-site request**: that describes cookies. The browser never attaches localStorage automatically; the API client adds the token itself.
- **Lost when the tab refreshes**: the opposite. localStorage survives a refresh; App.tsx reads it back on startup with readAuth.

excerpts.quote: | localStorage auth | `client/src/App.tsx:13-21` | Browser-side persistence; XSS risk. |
localStorage.setItem(authStorageKey, JSON.stringify(response));
useState<TokenResponse | null>(() => readAuth());

items.title: Why several API instances need a SignalR backplane
items.body:
**Key: a Redis backplane or Azure SignalR Service.**

SignalR keeps a live connection between each browser and one API process. When a message is posted, the endpoint publishes it to a group, but that process can only reach the connections it holds itself. With two or more API instances, a user connected to instance B would never hear a message posted through instance A. A backplane (Redis) or the hosted Azure SignalR Service passes each publish to every instance, so all connected clients receive it. The checklist asks for this before horizontal scaling, meaning before running more than one instance.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Sticky sessions only**: sticky sessions keep one user on one instance, but the sender and the listener can still be on different instances.
- **Move fanout into the React client**: the browser cannot reach other users' connections, and moving fanout to the client is not on the checklist.
- **Run SignalR in a separate SQLite file**: SignalR does not keep its connections in the database, and SQLite is itself on the list to be replaced.

excerpts.quote: Add Redis backplane or Azure SignalR Service before horizontal scaling.
await hub.Clients.Group(MessageHub.GroupName(channelId)).MessagePosted(message);

items.title: The Location header points at a route that does not exist
items.body:
**Key: it names /api/workspaces/{id}, a route that is not mapped.**

When a resource is created, a 201 response usually carries a Location header that says where to fetch the new thing. WorkspaceEndpoints returns Results.Created with the path /api/workspaces/ followed by the new workspace id. But the workspaces group maps only two routes: GET on "/" (list my workspaces) and POST on "/" (create). There is no GET for a single workspace by id. A client that follows the header gets a 404.

Why the others are wrong:
- **It is missing entirely**: Results.Created sets it; the problem is where it points.
- **It uses the slug instead of the id**: the code uses workspace.Id, not the slug.
- **It is relative, so the browser resolves it against the SPA host**: the finding says nothing about relative URLs; the issue is the unmapped route.

excerpts.quote: but the group maps only `GET /api/workspaces/` and `POST /api/workspaces/` (lines 14 and 17). Following the header yields 404.
return Results.Created($"/api/workspaces/{workspace.Id}", workspace);

items.title: Core idea: a check before a write can be out of date
items.body:
The astraupskill course is built around one classic bug: time-of-check to time-of-use.

Creating a workspace first asks the database "does this slug already exist?" If not, it adds the new workspace and saves. Between the question and the save there is a gap, and other requests can run in that gap.

As you read, draw a timeline with two requests for the same slug, interleaving their steps in the worst order you can find. Then find out which part of the system has the final say about duplicates, and what `WorkspaceService` does when its save fails: look at how it decides whether a failure is a slug conflict or something else.

Read 01-CODEBASE-MAP.md for the paths through CreateAsync, then 02-CONCEPTS.md for why the course prefers its approach over matching on error text.

excerpts.quote: Begin at [WorkspaceService.cs](../src/NetSlack.Application/Workspaces/WorkspaceService.cs).
# Concepts: CRUD, races, and boundaries

items.title: Start here: two guide sets, one Slack-style app
items.body:
NetSlack is a small Slack-like app: an ASP.NET Core API, EF Core over SQLite, SignalR for live messages, and a React client. This pack draws on two sets of guides in the repo.

**1. The architecture docs (read first).**
- **docs/architecture.md** - the four backend projects and what each owns, the frontend folders, and a production checklist.
- **docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md** - where input is checked and who decides what a user may do.
- **.../04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md** - what the app writes, what it only notifies, and what happens on failure.
- **.../06-architecture-critique.md** - strengths, ranked risks, and a three-month plan.

**2. The CRUD course in astraupskill/ (read second).** It follows one change: creating a workspace when two people race for the same slug. Its README gives the order, quoted below.

Every claim in these guides points at a file and line. Open those lines; reading the code next to the guide is how the ideas stick.

excerpts.quote: NetSlack is intentionally structured like a production product, not a tutorial toy.
Reading order: 01 map, 02 concepts, 03 worked change, 04 testing, 05 practice (each exercise has a **Check**), then 06 answers and verified review findings, 07 trace lab, and VERIFICATION.

readMore.why: Suggested paths through the larger upskill lab, by experience level.
The map of one workspace create, step by step.

items.title: A valid token says who you are, not what you may touch
items.body:
**Key: whether the service verifies the user's access to that specific resource.**

A JWT proves identity: the request comes from this user. It does not say whether this user belongs to the workspace or channel named in the request. That second question is authorization, and NetSlack answers it inside the application services. In ChannelService, EnsureWorkspaceMemberAsync looks up a WorkspaceMembers row for this workspace and this user, and throws ForbiddenException when there is none. The senior check is: for this exact resource id, is ownership or membership checked?

Why the others are wrong:
- **401 rather than 403**: getting the status right is good, but it does not tell you whether the access check exists at all.
- **Signing key length**: a strong key protects the token from forgery; a perfectly signed token still says nothing about membership.
- **Token expiry vs cookie**: expiry limits how long a token works, not which resources it may reach.

excerpts.quote: | "JWT means authorized." | Is resource ownership checked? Check `ChannelService.cs:56-62`. |
throw new ForbiddenException("You are not a member of this workspace.");

items.title: Saved message, failed publish: what the client sees
items.body:
**Key: a failed request, although the message was already durably saved.**

The message endpoint does two things in order. Line 33 calls service.PostAsync, which saves the message to the database. Line 34 then awaits the SignalR publish. If line 34 throws, the endpoint never reaches its return, so the exception goes to the error middleware and the client gets an error. But the save on line 33 has already committed. The database has the message; the client was told it failed. The guide's suggested fix is an outbox: write a "to publish" row with the message, and let a background dispatcher send it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Success after an automatic background retry**: the guide found no background services or retry library in the repo.
- **Success, because the hub swallows failures**: the publish is awaited in the endpoint; nothing catches its exception there.
- **Failed, and the save is rolled back**: the save already finished in PostAsync; there is no surrounding transaction that could undo it.

excerpts.quote: Request likely fails after durable write because publish is awaited in `src/NetSlack.Api/Endpoints/MessageEndpoints.cs:34`
var message = await service.PostAsync(channelId, new PostMessageCommand(request.Body), cancellationToken);
No `IHostedService`, `BackgroundService`, queue consumer, Polly retry, or `IHttpClientFactory` integration was found.

items.title: Two copies of one slug rule will drift apart
items.body:
**Key: if one copy changes, lookups stop matching the stored slug.**

WorkspaceService line 26 builds the slug with Trim, ToLowerInvariant and Replace, and uses that value for the precheck and for the recovery query. Workspace.Create, in the domain, stores the result of its own NormalizeSlug. Today both produce the same text. But they are two separate copies of one rule. If someone changes one of them, for example to collapse repeated dashes, the service would look up one string while the database stores another. The precheck would miss real duplicates and the recovery query would no longer recognise the winner, so the race handling breaks without any error. The fix is one normalisation function from the domain, used in all three places.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The domain copy always throws first**: the service copy runs first (line 26), before Workspace.Create is called on line 33.
- **It doubles the cost**: string trimming is cheap; the finding is about correctness, not speed.
- **Normalising twice breaks non-ASCII**: lowercasing an already lowercase string changes nothing; that is not the issue raised.

excerpts.quote: If either copy changes (say, collapsing repeated dashes), the precheck and recovery query look up a different key from the one that is stored, and the race classification silently breaks.
var slug = command.Slug.Trim().ToLowerInvariant().Replace(' ', '-');
var normalized = Guard.AgainstEmpty(slug, nameof(slug), 64)

items.title: Why a missing slug becomes a 500, not a 400
items.body:
**Key: 500, because the null slug throws NullReferenceException first.**

If the JSON body has no slug, model binding puts null into the Slug of CreateWorkspaceRequest. CreateAsync then runs line 26, which calls command.Slug.Trim(). Calling a method on null throws NullReferenceException. The domain's nicer check (Guard.AgainstEmpty, which throws ArgumentException) lives inside Workspace.Create, which would only run later, on line 33. The exception middleware maps ArgumentException to 400, but anything it does not recognise, including NullReferenceException, falls to the default case: 500.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400 from the domain's ArgumentException**: that check never gets a chance to run, because line 26 fails first.
- **409 because an empty slug collides**: no lookup happens; the code crashes before the precheck query.
- **201 with a slug derived from the name**: nothing in CreateAsync derives a slug from the name.

excerpts.quote: line 26 throws `NullReferenceException` before the domain's `ArgumentException` can run; `ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs:23-29` maps that to 500, not 400.
ArgumentException => StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest,

items.title: Why the unique index is still needed after the precheck
items.body:
**Key: two requests can both pass the precheck; only the index is race-safe.**

The precheck is a read: "is there a workspace with this slug?" Two requests arriving together can both read "no", because neither has saved yet. Both then try to insert. Only a rule enforced by the database at insert time can stop the second one, and that is the unique index on Slug in WorkspaceConfiguration. The validation guide lists the database as the layer for race-safe constraints, and the junior/senior table names this exact miss.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The index makes lookups fast enough to skip caching**: an index can speed up queries, but the guide gives it as a correctness constraint; caching is not mentioned.
- **EF skips the precheck when tracking is disabled**: tracking settings do not skip queries; the precheck in CreateAsync always runs.
- **The precheck only runs in development**: nothing in CreateAsync depends on the environment.

excerpts.quote: | "We already check slug exists." | Is there a unique index for races? Check `WorkspaceConfiguration.cs:17`. |
builder.HasIndex(workspace => workspace.Slug).IsUnique();
The unique database constraint is the final authority when two creates interleave.

items.title: Core idea: four backend projects, each with one job
items.body:
The backend is split into four C# projects. Learning which project owns what is the fastest way to find code.

- **NetSlack.Domain** holds the business nouns (workspace, channel, user, membership, message) and the facts that must always be true about them.
- **NetSlack.Application** holds the use cases: one service method per action, such as creating a workspace or posting a message.
- **NetSlack.Infrastructure** holds the technical plumbing: EF Core database code, JWT token creation and development seed data.
- **NetSlack.Api** holds the web layer: HTTP endpoints, the SignalR hub, middleware, CORS, health checks, Swagger and telemetry.

A good first exercise: pick one action, posting a message, and follow it from its endpoint in NetSlack.Api to the code that saves it. On the way, note where the "may this user post here?" check sits, what happens after the save, and in what order. Then read the validation-and-permissions guide and compare your notes with what it says.

excerpts.quote: `NetSlack.Domain` owns business concepts and invariants: workspaces, channels, users, memberships, and messages.
`NetSlack.Api` owns HTTP, SignalR, middleware, CORS, health checks, Swagger, and telemetry.
NetSlack is intentionally structured like a production product, not a tutorial toy.

readMore.why: A longer tour of the layer boundaries with code references.

items.title: AsNoTracking is not what makes the recovery query see the database
items.body:
**Key: no; DbSet queries run as SQL and never return pending entities.**

After a failed save, the recovery query asks AnyAsync on db.Workspaces whether the slug now exists. In EF Core, a LINQ query over a DbSet is always translated to SQL and sent to the database. It does not look at entities you have added but not yet saved. So the query already sees only committed rows, with or without AsNoTracking. AsNoTracking only means "do not track the objects this query returns", and AnyAsync returns a true/false, not objects. The call is harmless but does nothing here.

Why the others are wrong:
- **AnyAsync bypasses EF and runs raw SQL**: AnyAsync is an EF operator; EF translates it. The point is that it is translated, not that it bypasses EF.
- **Yes, EF merges the change tracker into results**: that is the exact misreading the finding warns about.
- **Yes, but only inside the same transaction**: the guide gives no such exception; pending entities are never returned by the query.

excerpts.quote: `AsNoTracking` only stops *materialized* results from being tracked, and `AnyAsync` materializes nothing.
.AnyAsync(existing => existing.Slug == slug, cancellationToken);

items.title: The P0 SignalR risk: joining any channel group
items.body:
**Key: that the caller may access the channel before joining its group.**

MessageHub has the Authorize attribute, so only a signed-in user can connect. But look at JoinChannel: it takes any channelId and immediately calls AddToGroupAsync. Nothing asks whether this user is a member of that channel. A signed-in user who knows or guesses a private channel's id could join its group and receive every new message published there. The critique marks it P0 and recommends checking the current user before AddToGroupAsync, plus an integration test. It says "may not verify" because the risk is read from the code, not proven by a test.

Why the others are wrong:
- **That the message text is non-empty**: messages are posted through MessageService, not through the hub; the hub only joins and leaves groups.
- **That groups are removed when a channel is deleted**: the critique does not raise this.
- **That the JWT is valid before connecting**: that part is covered; the Authorize attribute on the hub requires authentication.

excerpts.quote: return Groups.AddToGroupAsync(Context.ConnectionId, GroupName(channelId));
the hub requires authentication but no channel membership check appears in `src/NetSlack.Api/Hubs/MessageHub.cs:10-13`.

items.title: Which layer decides who may post to a channel
items.body:
**Key: NetSlack.Application, whose services enforce authorization.**

docs/architecture.md gives each project a job, and authorization belongs to the Application layer: its services accept commands, enforce authorization and return DTOs. You can see it in MessageService.PostAsync, whose first line calls EnsureCanPostChannelAsync before any message is created. Putting the rule there protects every way of reaching the use case, including a direct API call that skips the UI.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The React client hides the composer**: hiding a button is UX, not security. The validation guide's first junior miss is exactly "the button is hidden, so it is safe".
- **NetSlack.Api endpoint handlers**: the endpoints are deliberately thin; the message endpoint just calls the service and publishes the result.
- **The Message entity constructor**: the domain checks invariants of the message itself (such as its body), not whether a given user may post in a given channel.

excerpts.quote: `NetSlack.Application` owns use cases. Services accept commands, enforce authorization, and return DTOs.
var channel = await EnsureCanPostChannelAsync(channelId, cancellationToken);
| "The button is hidden, so it is safe." | Can a direct API request pass?

items.title: A retried post creates a second message today
items.body:
**Key: a second message is created, since posting is not idempotent.**

"Idempotent" means doing the same request twice has the same effect as doing it once. MessageService.PostAsync does not do that. Every call builds a brand new Message with Message.Post, adds it, and saves. Nothing in the request identifies "this is the same message as before", so the server cannot tell a retry from a new post. If the first attempt saved but the client timed out waiting, the retry saves a second copy. The guide suggests client-generated message ids or idempotency keys as the production fix.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Rejected with 409 because the text matches**: there is no uniqueness check on message text; two identical messages are allowed.
- **Server returns the first message by content hash**: no content hash or lookup exists in PostAsync.
- **The hub collapses both**: the hub only joins and leaves groups; each post is published separately.

excerpts.quote: Current message posting is not idempotent. If the client retries after a timeout, `src/NetSlack.Application/Messages/MessageService.cs:36-50` will create another message.
db.Messages.Add(message);

items.title: Where the checklist wants EF migrations applied
items.body:
**Key: in CI/CD, not on application startup.**

The production checklist in docs/architecture.md says to add EF migrations and apply them in the CI/CD pipeline. A migration is a script that changes the database schema. Running it as a separate, controlled deployment step means it happens once, can be reviewed, and can fail without taking the app down. Today there are no migrations at all: the development seeder calls EnsureCreated, which the critique lists as a P1 risk.

Why the others are wrong:
- **By the development seeder with EnsureCreated**: that is the current shortcut the checklist wants to replace. EnsureCreated builds a schema from scratch; it does not apply migrations.
- **Manually by an operator after each deploy**: the checklist names CI/CD, an automated pipeline, not a manual step.
- **On application startup**: the checklist explicitly says not on app startup.

excerpts.quote: Add EF migrations and apply them in CI/CD, not on app startup.
`src/NetSlack.Infrastructure/Seed/DevelopmentSeeder.cs:14` uses `EnsureCreated`
